# The Easy Method

> "Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind."
>
> — Romans 12:2

This book has one aim: to change the way you think about lust.

That's all. It won't make you stronger, and it won't make you more disciplined. It will change what you see when you look at porn, at the habit, and at the pull women have on you. Once you see it clearly, stopping is easy.

The usual way of quitting begins at the foot of a mountain. You stare up at it and take a deep breath. Then you spend weeks dragging yourself uphill, craving and feeling robbed. This way begins somewhere else. You begin with relief, like a man walking out of the doctor's office with the all-clear. And the feeling doesn't fade. Years from now you'll look back at this stretch of your life and scratch your head over why you ever did it. When you meet men who are still stuck, you'll feel sorry for them. You won't envy them for a second.

## No willpower campaign {-}

Until you've finished the whole book, don't start a willpower campaign.

Don't start a streak. Don't make a vow you'll break by Friday. Don't cut down to weekends. If you fall while you're reading, don't despair, and don't stop reading. And if the wish leaves you along the way, let it go, and don't call it back.

What this book rules out is the willpower vow. That is a promise made in your own strength, before you understand the trap. You've made that kind of promise before, and you know how long it lasts. The plain No at the end of this book is a different thing. You'll say it with your eyes open, and if you pray, you'll say it leaning on God.

Christian readers sometimes ask, "You've just told me it's a sin. Are you telling me to keep going?"

No. It is sin, and this book will never tell you to sin. Nobody is asking you to do it. If the wish has already gone, leave it gone. The instruction is only this: don't launch a willpower campaign halfway through a book that is about to make willpower unnecessary. You've already tried it that way, probably dozens of times. This time, do something you've never done before: watch yourself with your eyes open while the book explains what you're looking at. As you read, the wish to do it will shrink without any effort from you. Let it.

You may have stopped already. Or you may be a few days or weeks into a break and not know what to call yourself. Either way, stay stopped. In truth you're already free. The remaining chapters will let your head catch up with your hands.

By the way, there's no "one last time" ceremony waiting for you in the closing pages. The final step of this book is a decision you say out loud. For a believer it is a prayer, and there is a version for the man who doesn't pray. Either way, you'll be glad to say it.

## Why the normal way is so hard {-}

The normal way of quitting goes like this. You write down everything the habit costs you: the guilt, the tiredness, the lost time, the distance from God. Then you tell yourself:

"If I can just hold out long enough, the urge will finally die, and then I'll be happy."

It sounds sensible. Men do get free this way. But it is the hard road, and most men who take it end up where one man on a Christian forum did. He wrote that everything that depended on his own effort failed him sooner or later.

Here is why it's so hard.

**1. Stopping was never the problem.** You stop every single time you finish. In that flat, gray minute afterward, you are the most committed quitter on earth. "Never again. I mean it this time." Every man says it, and every man means it. The problem is not that minute. The problem is day three, or day thirty, or day three hundred, when you're tired or lonely and a quiet voice says "just this once". One becomes two, and you're back where you started, minus a little more self-respect. For some men it doesn't even take until day three. A nineteen-year-old, raised in a strict Christian home, wrote about his first time: "I vowed never to do that again, only to find myself searching for a secret place after a couple of hours."

**2. Guilt and fear make you reach for it.** What does a man do when he feels ashamed, anxious and worthless? He looks for comfort. And what has he trained himself to use for comfort? Tell a man the habit is ruining him and you've just handed him one more reason to escape into it tonight. A counselor on a Christian recovery blog saw it clearly: "Shame is the problem for so many, many Christians." This is why the scare videos and the thundering sermons have never freed you. They load the gun. A psychiatrist who treats porn addiction says the same from the clinic. A man who tries to quit out of desperation is doomed to fail, because desperation is the very thing that drives him back to it. He is talking about porn. It is just as true of the hand, and of the next woman you chase to feel better about yourself.

**3. Every reason to stop makes stopping harder.** That sounds mad, so take it slowly. For one thing, your reasons tell you that you *ought* to give something up. So part of you goes on believing there is something to give up: a comfort, a treat, an old friend. You feel like a man being marched away from his only pleasure. And for another, your reasons point your eyes at the wrong question. You don't do it because of the reasons you should stop. Nobody opens the site or shuts the bathroom door *because* it leaves him flat and guilty. The real question is the other one: why do you want to do it at all?

The man from the Christian forum, the one whose own effort failed him, spotted the trap inside all that effort. The harder he tried to stop thinking about porn, the more it became the center of his thoughts. Swap in "masturbation", or "her", and nothing changes.

Even the hard men of the internet have noticed. One coach has built a whole channel on discipline, and his advice on vices comes down to five words: "Do not rely on willpower."

## Three questions {-}

So for now we're going to put your reasons for stopping on a shelf. All of them, including the good ones, including the godly ones. We'll take them down again later, when they can no longer be used as a stick to beat you with.

In their place, look straight at what you do and ask:

1. **What is it actually doing for me?**
2. **Do I actually enjoy it?**
3. **Why am I doing this to myself?**

Here is the beautiful truth, and the rest of the book exists to prove it to you: lust does nothing for you. Nothing at all. The porn doesn't. The hand doesn't. The chase doesn't.

Be clear about what that means. I'm not saying the costs are bigger than the benefits. Every man already knows that, and it has never helped him. I'm saying there are no benefits.

Not one.

The relaxation, the sleep, the stress relief, the "release", the thrill of something new, the feeling of being wanted: each of them is an illusion. We'll take them apart one at a time.

The verse that opens this chapter comes from Paul, the apostle who wrote much of the New Testament. This is what he meant by "the renewing of your mind". He didn't say to try harder. He said "be transformed", which is something done to you, by God, as your mind is made new. If you're not a believer, call it changing your mind. Either way, it starts with seeing clearly.
